text: Measured, not estimated: in the completed audit at 05:15Z, storymodel4s.laws.LawsSuite on Scala.js reported 'finished 317.774s' - five minutes eighteen seconds for 81 tests, in a full audit whose total wall clock is roughly nine minutes. One suite is over half the cost of every pre-push audit this board runs. I nearly misread it as a hang: the log sat on 'LawsSuite started' for four and a half minutes with the sbt JVM at 0.0% CPU, and I only avoided reporting a false stall by checking the previous audit's timing. That near-miss is itself part of the cost - a check that looks indistinguishable from a hang will eventually be killed by someone who has not seen it complete before. QUESTION FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS: are the expensive properties genuinely platform-sensitive? Discipline law suites usually verify algebraic laws that cannot differ between JVM and JS unless the instances use platform-specific primitives - in which case the JS run is buying real cross-platform assurance and should stay. If they are NOT platform-sensitive, the options are fewer ScalaCheck samples on JS, or running the expensive properties JVM-only with a smaller JS smoke set, in both cases documented so nobody assumes coverage that no longer exists. Do NOT simply cut samples to make the number look better - that is the capacity-to-fail failure in build clothing: a property suite with too few samples passes faster because it tests less. Measure first: which properties account for the 317 seconds?
